samasa.vigraha: असम्यक् व्ययः शीलं येषां ते, तैः
samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (असम्यक् is a nañ tatpuruṣa: न सम्यक्)
samasa.literal: by those whose habit is improper spending
samasa.sense: by spendthrift, dishonest managers of the treasury

morph.note: Present third plural of √कृ (tanādi), weak stem कुरु- with u → v before the vowel ending: कुर्व्-अन्ति.
Present participle कुर्वत् (√कृ + śatṛ), instrumental plural: the t becomes d before bh. It agrees with तैः: ‘by them, making (expense)’.
The adjective ध्रुव ‘fixed, certain’ in the neuter accusative, used as an adverb: ‘surely’. The king is guessing, but with conviction.

mantras.anvaya: ते अद्य ध्रुवम् अन्यमहीभृताम् अनुवृत्तिं कुर्वन्ति। सततं व्ययं कुर्वद्भिः असम्यग्व्ययशीलैः तैः (1.16: …कोशः क्षयं गमिष्यति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the relative clause of 1.14 (ये … ते). The second line is a string of instrumentals whose verb, गमिष्यति, comes in 1.16.
mantras.lit: ‘— they surely now render service to other kings. By those given to improper spending, constantly making expenditure —
mantras.tr: surely they now pay court to other kings. And by those wastrels, spending without pause —

comm.t: The king imagines his former followers serving his rivals, and his ministers squandering his treasury. Both thoughts are guesses; he has no news.
A modern reading: anxiety supplies certainties (ध्रुवम्, ‘surely’) that the mind has no way of checking. Suratha suffers over events he can only imagine.

sandhi.note: Final t before c becomes c (एतच्च, अन्यच्च); च + अन्यत् → चान्यत्.

morph.note: Periphrastic perfect: roots with a derived stem (here the curādi चिन्तय-) form the perfect with -आम् + the perfect of √अस् (आस): चिन्तयाम् + आस. Compare अचिन्तयत् (imperfect) in 1.12, which opened the same train of thought.
Simple future of √गम् with connecting -इ-: गम् + इ + ष्य + ति. With क्षयम् ‘will go to ruin’.
Participle of सम् + √चि: ‘gathered together’. Printed with anusvāra for the nasal of सम् before c.

mantras.anvaya: (तैः) अतिदुःखेन संचितः सः कोशः क्षयं गमिष्यति। एतत् च अन्यत् च पार्थिवः सततं चिन्तयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence begun in 1.15b (‘through them … the treasury will go to ruin’); the second closes the king’s thoughts (1.12–16) and is the narrator’s.
mantras.lit: ‘— that treasury, amassed with great hardship, will go to ruin.’ This and other things the king pondered constantly.
mantras.tr: the treasury I gathered with such toil will be drained away.’ These and other thoughts filled the king’s mind without rest.
mantras.tr_note: ‘I’ is supplied: the Sanskrit says only ‘amassed with great hardship’.

comm.t: The last of the king’s worries is the treasury; the narrator then closes the passage: he thought of ‘this and other things’ ceaselessly. No इति marks the end of the thought; the change of verb (चिन्तयामास) does.
Suratha’s monologue moves through city, elephant, retainers and treasury — the things of a kingdom. Medhas’s later teaching treats all of them as objects of ममत्व held in place by Mahāmāyā.

samasa.literal: in the vicinity of the brahmin’s hermitage

morph.note: Passive participle of √प्रच्छ्: the root becomes पृच्छ्/प्रश्- and with -त gives पृष्ट (ś + t → ṣṭ). Verbs of asking take the person asked as the subject in the passive: ‘he was asked’.
Perfect of √दृश् with reduplication द- and guṇa of the root vowel (दृश् → दर्श्). Compare the aorist अद्राक्षीत् in 1.10.

mantras.anvaya: तत्र विप्राश्रमाभ्याशे सः एकं वैश्यं ददर्श। सः तेन पृष्टः — भोः, त्वं कः? अत्र आगमने च हेतुः कः?
mantras.anvaya_en: Two narrative clauses (the king saw; the merchant was asked) and the direct question, which continues into 1.18.
mantras.lit: There, near the brahmin’s hermitage, he saw a certain merchant. He was asked by him: ‘Who are you, sir? And what is the reason for your coming here?
mantras.tr: There, near the sage’s hermitage, he saw a merchant, and asked him: ‘Who are you, friend? What has brought you here?
mantras.tr_note: The passive (‘he was asked by him’) is turned into an active sentence.

comm.t: The second figure of the frame story appears: a merchant, met by chance near the hermitage. The king, absorbed in his own losses until now, notices another man’s grief and speaks first.

The meeting of the deposed king and the disowned merchant pairs two kinds of loss — power and family. The tradition reads the two as the seekers of enjoyment and of liberation, as their final requests in chapter 13 show.

samasa.sense: words said kindly, as to a friend

morph.note: Passive present, second singular, of √लक्ष्: ‘you are observed (as)’, i.e. ‘you look’. The predicates सशोकः and दुर्मनाः stand in the nominative with it.
Nominative singular masculine of the s-stem दुर्मनस्: the vowel before the final s is lengthened (-अस् → -आः).
Absolutive of a denominative verb formed from कर्ण ‘ear’; with the prefix आ it takes -य (lyap), and the stem’s -अय- is dropped: आकर्णय- → आकर्ण्य.

mantras.anvaya: त्वं कस्मात् सशोकः इव दुर्मनाः इव लक्ष्यसे? इति तस्य भूपतेः प्रणयोदितं वचः आकर्ण्य, (1.19: सः वैश्यः … प्रत्युवाच)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line ends the king’s question; इति closes it. The absolutive आकर्ण्य has as its subject the merchant of 1.19.
mantras.lit: ‘Why do you appear as if sorrowful, as if downcast?’ Having heard thus the words of that king, spoken in friendship —
mantras.tr: Why do you look so sorrowful, so heavy-hearted?’ Hearing these kindly words of the king,

comm.t: The king’s question ends, and the narrator notes its tone: it was spoken with प्रणय, warmth or friendliness. The repeated इव (‘as if’) is courteous; the king does not presume to name the stranger’s grief.
A modern reading: for the first time since 1.5 Suratha’s attention leaves his own losses. Concern for another’s sorrow opens the conversation that leads to the teaching.

अवनत is the kta of अव + √नम् ‘to bend’ (the nasal of नम् is lost before -त); active sense, ‘bowed’.

mantras.anvaya: सः वैश्यः प्रश्रयावनतः तं नृपं प्रत्युवाच।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject with its participle, the person addressed, and the verb. It completes the sentence of 1.18b (आकर्ण्य … प्रत्युवाच).
mantras.lit: — that merchant, bowed with humility, replied to that king.
mantras.tr: the merchant bowed respectfully and answered him.

comm.t: A half-śloka that closes the narrative of the meeting. The merchant answers with deference to a man he recognises as a king; his own story follows after the speaker label (1.20).
